faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Conway home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Conway?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: There is an alligator in our Myrtle Beach pond. Can you remove it?
faqs.a: No — and be wary of anyone in South Carolina who offers that as a routine service. Alligators are state-listed as Threatened here and are handled only through SCDNR's program: nuisance alligators are reported to SCDNR, which issues tags and permits to property owners or sends a contracted Alligator Control Agent. What we can do in Myrtle Beach is the safety side: keep people and pets back from pond edges near oceanfront resort corridor, never feed an alligator, and call SCDNR promptly if one is acting as a nuisance.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Surfside Beach lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Surfside Beach home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: A skunk is living under my Little River deck. How is that handled?
faqs.a: A skunk under a deck wants two things: shelter and grubs, and Little River yards near Intracoastal Waterway waterfront and marsh creeks at the county's north end supply both. We set covered traps right at the den entrance to keep the animal calm, remove it under depredation rules, and then bury hardware cloth along the deck edge so the den cannot be re-dug. Skunks rank second only to raccoons in SC Department of Public Health rabies testing, which is why we do not recommend reaching, prodding, or trying to smoke one out.

faqs.q: Mole tunnels are tearing up my Little River yard. Can you stop them?

We trap on the active travel tunnels, confirmed by pressing a section down and checking it the next day, rather than scattering repellents that only move the animal to the next yard. In sandy soil near Intracoastal Waterway waterfront and marsh creeks at the county's north end, fresh tunnels can appear overnight after rain.

Little River.wildlife_intro:
What makes Little River different from the next town over is the Intracoastal Waterway waterfront and marsh creeks at the county's north end. More than anything else, we are called for raccoons denning above ceilings and opossums working the crawlspace piers.

Historic raised homes, tabby and brick cottages, and modern subdivisions on filled ground make for three different exclusion jobs on a single street. Salt marsh, tidal creeks, and live oaks draped in Spanish moss shape the work here: animals travel the marsh edge at low tide, shelter under raised houses between tides, and push inland ahead of king tides and summer storms.

The last step on a Little River call is a walk-around with the homeowner: each entry we sealed, each burrow we screened, and what to watch for when the seasons turn.
